question: Does correct spatial information provide a larger benefit as the number of sampled neurons increases?
dataset: Stringer MP019, visual cortex; one recording, not whole brain
coordinate_assignment: all coordinate assignments fixed for the full run; shuffle moves coordinates only, keeping neural activity, IDs and speed unchanged
nested_pools: each pool sampled without replacement once at 2048 cells; prefixes define smaller populations; independent pools can overlap
coordinate_normalization: fixed mean/std across all eligible cells, shared across population sizes and conditions; no behavioral targets used
architecture: MLP activity encoder, ID embedding, coordinate MLP, 8 learned latents, one width-32 transformer layer, 4 heads, dropout 0.05, mean pooling and linear speed head
training: 24 epochs maximum; AdamW lr0.001, weight_decay0.01, cosine minlr0.0001, batch32, gradient norm clip1; early stop after >=12 epochs and 7 stale epochs
splits: same chronological train/validation/test and common target index31 as previous search; test already examined historically, exploratory replication only
primary_contrasts: paired test MSE(shuffled)-MSE(real) and MSE(none)-MSE(real), positive favors correct coordinates; also report validation and raw MSE
density_interaction: contrast at 2048 minus contrast at128 for the same pool and optimizer seed; positive favors an increasing spatial benefit
evidence_gate: real must beat both shuffled and none on mean test MSE at2048, with a positive mean advantage in each of the three pools; growing-benefit claim additionally needs positive density interaction in each pool; no generalization beyond this recording regardless of gate
secondary_controls: depth-only and within-depth shuffled x/y at2048; these are predeclared descriptive controls
budget: 66 neural fits:54 primary and12 depth controls; all configurations frozen before any new result; one short synthetic positive control for the exercised architecture
